1. CALL TO ORDER

Chair Huff called the meeting to order at 6:32 p.m.

2. ROLL CALL

COMMITTEE MEMBERS PRESENT
Chair Britt Huff  William Larson
Bridget Carman  Cat Spydell
Debora Chan-Southwell  Bob Schachter
Debby Stegura

COMMITTEE MEMBERS ABSENT
Lou Persichina

STAFF MEMBERS PRESENT
Alexa Davis, Assistant to the City Manager
Jeannie Naughton, Senior Planner
Kelley Thom, Associate Planner

3. APPROVAL OF MINUTES

TO APPROVE THE MINUTES OF September 14, 2015.  There being no objection,
Chairwoman Huff so ordered.

4. AUDIENCE ITEMS NOT ON THE AGENDA

Member Spydell brought up the coyote sighting issue. Due to increased discussion on the site
NextDoor, she indicated that the City needs to do something but there are limits as to what can
be done. She explained that when one starts "trapping" or killing it can actually make things
worse; she is hoping to put together a coyote awareness program; Member Spydell said she
personally hazes at her home and it effectively keeps coyotes off of her property. Staff
explained that the City established a Coyote Management and went into contract with the
County of Agriculture around the year 2010 and that due to earlier than normal calls reporting
coyotes, the City has been ramping up coyote awareness education to the Community.

Member Larson indicated that the County service was very effective in his case a few years
ago.

Chair Huff explained that her neighborhood is experiencing more coyotes than in past. She
believes the drought is likely impacting the population as coyotes move out of the natural habitat
looking for food.

DRAFT Environmental Advisory Committee Minutes  1
April 19, 2016
 Member Carman believes that all wildlife has increased due the development changes at the
golf course. She personally has kept up responsibility with her animals and feels that all
residents need to take that responsibility. She feels that the current Coyote Management Plan
is effective.

The full committee agreed that the City should continue providing awareness as to coyote
management, in particular tips on how to keep coyotes away from pets, personal animals and
property.

5.  NEW BUSINESS

  A. GRAY WATER -

Staff Member Thom provided an overview of the written staff report. She explained that a
plumbing permit is needed the more involved the system it gets; however a simple system
(example: laundry to landscape) a permit is not needed. She further explained that non-potable
is ok to be used but should not be sprayed and dispersed in the air. One important aspect of
gray water is knowing what goes into the water and what is being output.

Staff Member Thom detailed permitting information through the County as documented within
the staff report attachment. She further explained that permitting is a combination of the Health
and Building Departments. She stated that no one in the City has applied for a gray water permit
to date.

Member Spydell suggested that the share information with the public on the gray water process.

Chair Huff agreed with Member Spydell and also asked if studies are needed for gray water soil
quality. Staff Member Kelley responded that it may not be needed, however knowing the pH of
soil may be helpful so you ensure you are not killing any landscape or plants.

Chair Huff explained that gray water systems would help the City reduce its target water
reduction. Member Spydell agreed and also stated that collecting water, such as rain water,
can also help.

It was a consensus of the committee to receive and file this report and to share more
information about the gray water process with the public through regular means of
communication.

6.  OLD BUSINESS

  A.  DROUGHT UPDATE

Staff member Davis highlighted the written staff report. She explained that the Governor’s water
reduction is still in effect through February 2016 and that the City, as part of the Palos Verdes
Service area of California Water Service (“CalWater”) is required to reduce water consumption
by 36%. Staff Member Davis also explained that the City adopted a Water Restriction Level 2
effective August 1, 2015 which is still in effect.

DRAFT Environmental Advisory Committee Minutes  2
April 19, 2016
 Member Spydell has been working with CalWater for her personal budget and explained that
she had success earlier on in the process but was having difficulty getting to a final resolution.
She explained that the public should be aware and be diligent in keeping in communication with
CalWater if there needs to be any modification to the water budget.

It was a consensus of the Committee to receive and file this report and remind the community
about the restrictions and water budget in the coming months.

  B. ENERGY EMISSIONS CLIMATE ACTION PLAN (EECAP)

Staff Member Davis provided a brief overview of the written report and explained that the City
worked with the South Bay Cities Council of Governments (SBCCOG) to finalize the Energy
Efficiency Chapter of the Climate Action Plan (EECAP) which is to serve as the City’s roadmap
for reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in City operations and the community at large.
The report that was provided to the Committee was a final version provided to Southern
California Edison as part of the grant process and incorporates GHG data as well as energy
efficiency measures the City adopted in 2015.

Member Spydell was surprised to see how high the fleet emissions were in the Report and
though this number would be adjusted to reflect the appropriate data from the City. Staff
Member Davis explained she would contact the SBCCOG to go over this in order for it to be
updated in future reports. Member Spydell asked if the Sherriff fleet was included in the data;
Staff responded that it is not.

Member Carman asked if there could be more consideration toward electric vehicle charging
stations in the City. Staff Member Thom responded that there will be 3-4 stations installed at
the Promenade over time. Chair Huff indicated that the City of Torrance has increased their
charging stations. Member Carman expressed that there is not enough stations to help sustain
electric vehicles and suggested that there be stations available at City Hall and other City
facilities as well as installed at any new development. Staff Member Thom explained that
electric vehicle charging is required for new residential developments currently. Member
Stegura asked if it can be considered for the Village project at the shared library parking lot and
if there are any potential sponsors like Toyota or Honda, since they are local companies.

It was recommended that this report be received and filed and that staff further assess the
ability to install electric vehicle charging stations and facilities and consider the options of
requiring them at commercial areas. Moved by Member Stegura and Seconded by Member
Carman. All Committee members were in favor.

  C. COMMUNITY CHOICE AGGREGATION (CCA) UPDATE

Senior Planner Naughton gave a brief overview of Community Choice Aggregation (CCA)
consistent with the staff report. She explained that Southern California Edison (SCE) has been
very cooperative with the process that has now become a full-county effort. She further
explained that if the County implemented CCA, it would be the largest power company in the
country and would account for 50% of SCE's power delivery.

DRAFT Environmental Advisory Committee Minutes  3
April 19, 2016
 Member Stegura asked if will they sell bonds to finance it. Staff Member Naughton explained
she is not aware if that is an option at this time.

Staff Member Naughton explained that the County expects to complete the feasibility study in
May; if the study shows that CCA is potentially viable for the County and its jurisdictions, they
will use that study to leverage significant investments from larger banks, such as Goldman
Sachs, for more detailed technical studies, program development and start-up costs.

Chair Huff asked about the background of the individual who has been coordinating the effort,
Joe Galiano. Staff Member Naughton said she did not have this detailed information but can
bring it back at a future date.

Member Larson said he was interested and concerned about home solar and particularly
neighborhoods that are solar and wondered if it had been discussed. Staff Member Naughton
responded that the feasibility study is looking at larger sites that can be developed as renewable
energy sources. Member Larson explained that it was being done at schools and businesses
establishments.

Staff Member Naughton explained that nothing would change as part of power delivery; SCE
would deliver the energy and continue to bill customers. Rate payers would be given the option
to opt-out of the program, or choose between a tiered system of renewable energy (how much
of their energy would be from renewable energy sources).

Member Carman asked about the benefits of CCA. Staff Member Naughton responded that
CCA allows local governments to pool their electricity load in order to purchase renewable
energy for their constituents, as well as invest in new, local renewable power development. CCA
works with the existing utility infrastructure, allows for more competitive rates, transitioning to a
cleaner and more efficient energy supply, while creating local jobs. While utility companies like
SCE are Investor Owned Utilities (IOUs), CCAs are non-profit Joint Power Authorities, allowing
for excess profits to be re-invested into the program to keep rates low, and for investment in the
creation of new renewables development, rather than those profits being distributed to
investors.

Member Carman asked if the CCA is responsible for generating the electricity. Staff responded
that they are only responsible for buying the energy, but it may also become involved in
investment into land acquisition for the creation of local, renewable energy development.
Member Carman confirmed that Southern California Edison would continue to deliver the
energy purchased by the CCA.

Member Carman asked about the climate on the business development side. Staff responded
that the feasibility study will assess that question and it is expected that any money invested in
initial start-up costs would be paid back in the first year.

Member Carman asked why jurisdictions such as the City of Santa Monica are against utilizing
unbundled Renewable Energy Credits (RECs). Staff Member Naughton explained that it is like
a cap and trade program; a REC is a certificate that certifies energy was created from a
renewable source—the developer can sell the energy created from the renewable source, along
with the REC (bundled), or if regulations allow, the developer can sell the energy and REC
separately (unbundled). Those that oppose unbundled RECs argue that it allows utilities to
utilize non-renewable energy, while receiving credit for renewable energy, and the practice does
not promote locally-sourced renewable energy, nor the creation of new, renewable developers.

DRAFT Environmental Advisory Committee Minutes  4
April 19, 2016
 Member Stegura asked if there has been any discussion whether SCE would charge more for
delivery to homes. For example, if one is using solar, even if they’re generating more power
than they use, SCE is charging solar customers a standard fee for use of the infrastructure.
She wondered if there is a possibility that SCE would raise that fee. Staff indicated at this time
they were unaware of any potential changes but it may be a consideration of SCE in the future.

It was a consensus of the Committee to receive and file this report.

7.  COMMITTEE ITEMS/FUTURE AGENDAS ITEMS

Staff Member Davis mentioned that the City’s Earth Day Celebration would be held on
Wednesday, April 20 and that this year’s event included the City of Rancho Palos Verdes and
Rolling Hills.

Staff Member Davis also mentioned that there is currently a vacancy on this Environmental
Advisory Committee and interested parties can contact Deputy City Clerk, Hope Nolan, for more
information.

Staff Member Davis explained that the Street Light Retrofit project is still being reviewed by staff
in coordination with the South Bay Environmental Services Center but the project would not
change full light posts, only retrofit the bulbs with LED lights. Staff would keep the Committee
updated on any progress.

Member Carman asked about the Palos Verdes Unified School District solar project and
wondered how the City can learn from it and/or catch that wave. Member Stegura gave a brief
overview that solar panels are being planned at every school site but there has been some
community push back as to the process in securing a vendor. She further explained that many
school sites are wanting the solar panel structures which will provide energy sources reducing
utility costs and also provide overall shade for the campus.

Member Carman also mentioned that the gas tax that cities use to improve roads may be less
revenue in the future as vehicles are less reliant on gas and suggested that the City consider
other resources.

8.  ADJOURNMENT

Chair Huff adjourned the meeting at 7:52 p.m.

Respectfully submitted,

Alexa D. Davis
Assistant to the City Manager

   ITEM 5 A.

  Staff Report

DATE:  JULY 11, 2016

TO:  ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE

FROM:  ALEXA DAVIS, ASSISTANT TO THE CITY MANAGER

SUBJECT:  DROUGHT UPDATE; CITY WATER CONSERVATION
  MEASURES

OVERVIEW

This report provides a general update of the State drought restrictions and the City of
Rolling Hills Estates’ response to water reduction requirements.

BACKGROUND

Governor Brown issued an Executive Order in April 2015 which required a mandatory
statewide water use reduction of 25%. In response, the State Water Resources Control
Board (SWRCB) released regulations proposing that cities on the Peninsula, including
the City of Rolling Hills Estates, reduce water use by 36% by February 2016. The City’s
water supplier, California Water Service (“Cal Water”), established regulations for its
customers in order to meet the 36% target, which was effective June 1, 2015.

In response to the State order and to be consistent with Cal Water’s regulations, the City
enacted Ordinance No. 699, a revised and amended Water Conservation Ordinance, and
Resolution No. 2353 Declaring Level 2 Water Restriction, which took effect on August 1,
2015 (Attachment A).

Since the last Environmental Advisory Committee meeting in April, the State Water
Resources Board adopted revisions to its emergency drought regulation called for by
Governor Brown’s May 9, 2016 Executive Order, which contained two essential elements,
aimed at making water conservation a way of life in California. First, the regulations retain
each of the existing prohibitions on certain uses of potable water, including the “irrigation
with potable water of ornamental turf on public street medians.” Second, the revised
regulations move away from conservation standards crafted by the State and toward
conservation targets based upon local water supply conditions. Specifically, the revised
regulations require water utilities to conduct a “stress test” of their water supplies based
on a formula established by the Board.

  1
 As a result, Cal Water will be making some adjustments to its Drought Response Plan
based upon their analysis that modest demand reductions are needed to meet expected
demand over the next three years, even with future dry years ahead. Despite this, much
of the state continues to experience severe drought conditions and there is a distinct
likelihood that there will be an extremely dry winter, exacerbating existing drought
conditions.

For the Palos Verdes Service area, Cal Water will be establishing an interim water-use
reduction requirement of 10% for customers (versus the 36% previously required). The
revised conservation target effectively balances the improved water supply conditions
brought about by this past winter’s precipitation and the need to prepare for the possibility
of an extremely dry winter. Concurrent with establishing new water conservation targets,
Cal Water is proposing to the Public Utilities Commission to move from Stage 2 to Stage
1 of their Schedule 14.1 Water Shortage Contingency plan, which will allow them to
suspend the Drought Surcharges of those customers who exceed their monthly water
budgets. However, customers will continue to see their monthly water-use targets on
their water utility bills to assist them in meeting the new interim conservation
targets. These targets will continue to be based on a customer’s same-month water
usage from 2013, except for unique situations.

Cal Water recommends that the City remain at Level 2 of the Water Conservation and
Water Shortage Management Plan as a prudent approach towards water conservation.
Representatives from Cal Water will be in attendance at the Monday’s meeting.

ANALYSIS

With the updated State regulations and the proposed modifications to Cal Water’s
Schedule 14.1 Water Shortage Contingency Plan, the Environmental Advisory
Committee may want to revisit the City’s currently adopted water shortage response level
(Level 2) to determine if it should remain at the same level or be reduced to Level 1.

RECOMMENDATION

This is a matter of Committee discretion.

  2. Cal Water Letter

Editor's note—Ord. No. 699, § 3, adopted July 14, 2015, effectively repealed the former Ch. 13.04, §§
13.04.010—13.04.130, and Exh. A to said ordinance enacted a new Ch. 13.04 as set out herein. The
former Ch. 13.04 pertained to similar subject matter and derived from Ord. No. 650, § 1, adopted Feb. 24,
2009. See also the Code Comparative Table.

13.04.010 - Title.

  This chapter is known as the City of Rolling Hills Estates Water Conservation and Water Shortage
Management Plan.

(Ord. No. 699, § 3(Exh. A), 7-14-2015)

13.04.020 - Declaration of policy.

  The city declares that because of frequent water shortage conditions prevailing in the city and in the
areas of this state and elsewhere from which the city obtains its water supplies, the general welfare requires
that the water resources available to the city's water customers be put to the maximum beneficial use, and
that the waste or unreasonable use or unreasonable method of use of water be prevented, and the
conservation of such water is to be exercised with a view towards reasonable and beneficial uses that are
in the best interests of the city's residents, businesses and visitors.

(Ord. No. 699, § 3(Exh. A), 7-14-2015)

13.04.030 - Declaration of purpose.

  The purpose of this chapter is to enhance water conservation planning, maximize the use of recycled
water and provide a water shortage management plan that maximizes the efficient use of potable and
recycled water to minimize the effects of a shortage of water within the city and reduce the consumption of
water provided by the city's water retailer, California Water Service Company, thereby extending available
water supplies, while reducing the hardships on the city and the general public to the greatest extent
possible.

(Ord. No. 699, § 3(Exh. A), 7-14-2015)

13.04.040 - Water conservation and water shortage management plan establishment and application.

A.  This chapter establishes regulations related to water use efficiency to be implemented during times of
  declared water shortages or declared water shortage emergencies. The chapter provides four levels

  Page 1
   of water shortage response actions to be implemented in times of shortage, with increasing restrictions
  on water use in response to worsening water shortage conditions and decreasing available supplies.
B.  The provisions of this chapter apply to any person or business in the use of any water provided by the
  city's water retailer.
C.  This chapter is intended solely to further the conservation of water. It is not intended to implement any
  provision of federal, state, or local statutes, ordinances or regulations relating to protection of water
  quality or control of drainage or runoff.
D.  Nothing in this chapter applies to the use of water that is subject to a special supply program, if
  applicable.
E.  The provisions of this chapter do not apply to the use of water from private wells.

(Ord. No. 699, § 3(Exh. A), 7-14-2015)

13.04.050 - Permanent water conservation measures.

  The following water conservation measures are in effect at all times:
  A.  Excessive Water Flow or Runoff. Watering in a manner that results in overspray or excessive
  runoff onto paved or hardscaped areas is prohibited.
  B.  Water Fountains and Decorative Water Features. Water fountains and decorative water features
  must have a water recirculation system.
  C.  No Watering After Measurable Rainfall. Watering any lawn or landscape area at any time within
  forty-eight hours after a measurable rainfall is prohibited. For the purposes of this regulation, a
  "measurable rainfall" means at least .25 inches of rainfall over a twenty-four-hour period based
  on the rainfall precipitation map maintained by the Los County Department of Public Works, Water
  Resource Division, for the monitoring location listed as "Rolling Hills" or, if such station is
  eliminated, then the monitoring station closest to the city's boundary will be used. These
  measurements  can  be  accessed  at  the  following  website:
  http://www.ladpw.org/wrd/storms/index.cfm.
  D.  Repair of Leaks. No person may permit or cause to permit the excess use, loss or escape of
  water through breaks, leaks or other malfunctions in the water user's plumbing or distribution
  system for any period of time after such escape of water should have reasonably been discovered
  or corrected. All leaks must be repaired upon discovery, but no later than within seventy-two hours
  of notification by the city or the city's water retailer unless other arrangements are made with the
  city or the city's water retailer.
  E.  Washing Vehicles. Washing any automobile, truck, van, bus, motorcycle, boat or any other
  vehicle is restricted to the use of a hand-held bucket or similar container or a hand-held hose
  equipped with a positive self-closing water shut-off nozzle or device. This provision does not apply
  to a commercial car washing facility.
  F.  Washing Hard or Paved Surfaces. Washing of hard or paved surfaces, including sidewalks,
  walkways, driveways, parking areas, tennis courts, patios or alleys, is prohibited except when
  necessary to alleviate safety or sanitary hazards or as surface preparation for the application of
  any architectural coating or painting. All such permitted washing must be done by use of a hand-
  held bucket or similar container, a hand-held hose equipped with a positive self-closing water
  shut-off device, a low-volume, high-pressure cleaning machine, or a low-volume high-pressure
  waterbroom.

(Ord. No. 699, § 3(Exh. A), 7-14-2015)

13.04.060 - Water shortage response level 1 measures.

  Page 2
   In addition to all permanent measures, the following additional water conservation measures apply
during a declared level 1 condition:
  A.  Drinking Water Served on Request. All eating and drinking establishments of any kind, including
  any restaurant, hotel, cafe, cafeteria, bar or club, whether public or private, may only provide
  drinking water to any person upon an express request.
  B.  Restaurants Required to Use Water Conserving Technology. All eating and drinking
  establishments that require washing or cleaning of kitchen or dining room area flooring must do
  so using a hand-held bucket or similar container, a mop using bucket or similar container, or
  "waterbroom" technologies. Such establishments must also utilize water conserving nozzles on
  pre-rinse spray valves.
  C.  Commercial Lodging Establishment Linen Service. All hotels, motels, or bed and breakfasts must
  provide customers with an option of choosing to have towels and linens laundered daily. The
  establishment must prominently display notice of this option in each bathroom and sleeping room
  using clear and easily understood language.
  D.  Commercial Car Wash Businesses. On or after January 1, 2012, all "conveyor" style car wash
  systems must have and maintain water recycling systems.

(Ord. No. 699, § 3(Exh. A), 7-14-2015)

13.04.070 - Water shortage response level 2.

  In addition to all permanent measures and all measures listed under response level 1, the following
additional water conservation measures apply during a declared level 2 condition:
  A.  Watering Limited to Three Days a Week. Residential and commercial landscape irrigation is
  limited to no more than three assigned days per week based on a schedule established by the
  city's water retailer. This section does not apply to commercial growers or nurseries.

(Ord. No. 699, § 3(Exh. A), 7-14-2015)

13.04.080 - Water shortage response level 3.

  In addition to all permanent measures and all measures listed under response levels 1 and 2, the
following additional water conservation measures apply during a declared level 3 condition:
  A.  Watering Limited to Two Days a Week. Residential and commercial landscape irrigation is limited
  to no more than two assigned days per week on a schedule established by the city's water retailer.
  This section does not apply to commercial growers or nurseries.
  B.  Filling or Refilling Ornamental Lakes or Ponds. The filling or refilling or of ornamental lakes or
  ponds is prohibited except to the extent needed to sustain aquatic life, provided that such animals
  are of significant value and have been actively managed within the water feature prior to
  declaration of a water shortage response level under this chapter. The city may also implement
  a moratorium on building permits issued for such ornamental lakes or ponds.
  C.  Washing Vehicles. The washing of vehicles is prohibited except at commercial car washes.
  D.  Repair of Water Leaks. All water leaks must be repaired upon discovery, but no later than within
  forty-eight hours of notification by the city or the city's water retailer unless other arrangements
  are made with the city or the water retailer.
  E.  Use of Water for Construction Purposes. The use of potable water for construction purposes,
  such as consolidation of backfill, dust control, or other uses is prohibited unless the city is provided
  with substantial evidence that no other source of water or other method can be used.

  Page 3
   F.  Filling or Refilling of Pools. The refilling and initial filling of single-family residential swimming
  pools or outdoor spas with potable water is prohibited.

(Ord. No. 699, § 3(Exh. A), 7-14-2015)

13.04.090 - Water shortage response level 4.

  In addition to all permanent measures and all measures listed under response levels 1, 2 and 3, the
following additional water conservation measures apply during a declared level 4 condition:
  A.  Landscape Irrigation. Landscape irrigation is prohibited, except crops and landscape products of
  commercial growers and nurseries. If the city determines that recycled water is available, it may
  be applied for the following uses:
  1.  Maintenance of trees and shrubs that are watered by using a bucket, hand-held hose with a
  positive shut-off nozzle, or low-volume non-spray irrigation.
  2.  Maintenance of existing landscaping necessary for fire protection as specified by the fire
  marshal of the local fire protection agency having jurisdiction over the property to be irrigated.
  3.  Maintenance of existing landscaping for erosion control.
  4.  Maintenance of plant materials identified to be rare or essential to the well-being of rare
  animals.
  5.  Maintenance of landscaping within active public parks and playing fields, day care centers,
  school grounds, cemeteries, and golf course greens, provided that such irrigation does not
  exceed two days per week.
  6.  Public works projects and actively irrigated environmental mitigation projects.
  B.  Leaks. All water leaks must be repaired within twenty-four hours of detection or notification by the
  city or the city's water retailer unless other arrangements are made with the city or the water
  retailer.
  C.  No New Potable Water Service. No new potable water service will be provided, no new temporary
  meters or permanent meters will be provided, and no statements of immediate ability to serve or
  provide potable water service (such as will-serve letters, certificates, or letters of availability) will
  be issued, except under any of the following circumstances:
  1.  A valid, unexpired building permit has been issued for the project.
  2.  The project is necessary to protect the public health, safety, and welfare.
  3.  The applicant provides substantial evidence of an enforceable commitment that water
  demands for the project will be offset prior to the provision of a new water meter to the
  satisfaction of city.
  This provision will not be construed to preclude the resetting or turn-on of meters to provide
  continuation of water service or to restore service that has been interrupted for a period of one year or
  less.
  D.  Limits on Building Permits. The city will withhold the issuance of any new building permit that
  requires new or expanded water service, except to protect the public health, safety and welfare,
  or in situations that satisfy the city's adopted water conservation offset requirements.
  E.  No New Annexations. The city will suspend consideration of annexations to its service area. This
  provision does not apply to boundary corrections and annexations that will not result in any
  increased use of water.

(Ord. No. 699, § 3(Exh. A), 7-14-2015)

  Page 4
 13.04.100 - Procedures for determination and notification of water shortage response level.

A.  The existence of water shortage response level 1, level 2, level 3 or level 4 condition may be declared
  by resolution of the city council adopted at a regular or special public meeting held in accordance with
  state law and with consultation from the city's water retailer and wholesaler. The mandatory
  conservation measures applicable to water shortage response level 1, level 2, level 3 or level 4
  conditions will take effect on the tenth day after the date the response level is declared. The city will
  publish a copy of the resolution in a newspaper used for publication of official notices.
B.  The city may declare an end to a water shortage response level by the adoption of a city council
  resolution at any regular or special meeting held in accordance with state law.

(Ord. No. 699, § 3(Exh. A), 7-14-2015)

13.04.110 - Hardship exemption.

A.  If, due to unique circumstances, a specific requirement of this chapter would result in undue hardship
  to a person using water or to property upon which water is used that is disproportionate to the impacts
  to water users generally or to similar property or classes of water uses, then the person may apply for
  an exemption to the requirements of this chapter.
B.  The exemption may be granted or conditionally granted, only upon a written finding of the existence
  of facts demonstrating an undue hardship to a person using water or to property upon which water is
  used, that is disproportionate to the impacts to water users generally or to similar property or classes
  of water use due to specific and unique circumstances of the user or the user's property.
  1.  Application. An application for an exemption must be in a form prescribed by the city and must
  be accompanied by a nonrefundable processing fee in an amount set by city council resolution.
  2.  Supporting Documentation. The application must be accompanied by photographs, maps,
  drawings, and other information, including a written statement of the applicant.
  3.  Required Findings for Exemption. An application for an exemption will be denied unless the
  approving authority finds, based on the information provided in the application, supporting
  documents, or such additional information as may be requested, and on water use information
  for the property as shown by the records of the city or the city's water retailer, all of the following:
  (a) That the exemption does not constitute a grant of special privilege inconsistent with the
  limitations upon other residents and businesses;
  (b) That because of special circumstances applicable to the property or its use, the strict
  application of this chapter would have a disproportionate impact on the property or use that
  exceeds the impacts to residents and businesses generally;
  (c) That the authorizing of an exemption will not be of substantial detriment to adjacent
  properties, and will not materially affect the ability of the city to effectuate the purpose of this
  chapter and will not be detrimental to the public interest; and
  (d) That the condition or situation of the subject property or the intended use of the property for
  which the exemption is sought is not common, recurrent or general in nature.
  4.  Approval Authority. The city manager or designee may exercise approval authority and act upon
  any completed application for an exemption no later than ten days after submittal and may
  approve, conditionally approve, or deny the exemption request. The applicant requesting the
  exemption will be promptly notified in writing of any action taken. Unless specified otherwise at
  the time an exemption is approved, the exemption applies to the subject property during the term
  of the applicable mandatory water shortage response declaration.
  5.  Appeals to City Council. An applicant for an exemption may appeal a decision or condition of the
  city on an application to the city council within ten days of the decision upon written request for a

  Page 5
   hearing. The request must state the grounds for the appeal. At a public meeting, the city council
  will act as the approval authority and review the appeal de novo by following the procedure utilized
  for applications for variances. The decision of the city council is final.

(Ord. No. 699, § 3(Exh. A), 7-14-2015)

13.04.120 - Penalties and remedies.

  Any person who uses, causes to be used, or permits the use of water in violation of this chapter is
guilty of an offense punishable as follows:
  1.  The first violation of any provision of this chapter will constitute an infraction whereby a written
  warning will be issued to the party or parties that committed the infraction.
  2.  The second violation of any provision of this chapter will constitute an infraction punishable by a
  fine not to exceed one hundred dollars. Each day that a violation occurs will constitute a separate
  offense.
